evidence: Independent review in my own context (preflight bundle reports/mindmap-pass/2026-11-14-trend-lane-c-run/preflight-chart-review, 31/31 parts read, check returned delivery-complete-sources-current; actor mindmap-chart-review-lane-c, context trend-lane-c-2026-11-14-review, epoch 1). (1) Primary sources: I re-fetched 26 USC 72 and 26 USC 4975 and 26 USC 416 from Cornell LII on 2026-11-14 (HTTP 200) and compared the text to research/statute-extracts.md. 72(p)(2)(A)(i)-(ii), (B), (C), 72(p)(3) match. 4975(d)(1)(A)-(E) matches. 4975(f)(6)(A) and (B)(i)(II)-(III) and (B)(iii) match verbatim, so the BUILD finding that the loan exclusion for owner-employees only covers IRA-type owners is correct: a solo 401(k) owner is not categorically barred from a plan loan, while an IRA-based plan (SEP, SIMPLE, traditional IRA) cannot lend to its owner. (2) The statute reading exposes a real defect in the TL-01 answer sentence: the statute limits new loan plus all outstanding loans to the lesser of A = $50,000 less (highest 12-month balance minus current outstanding balance) and B = greater of half vested or $10,000, so max new loan = min($50,000 - highest12, B - outstanding). The manifest answer says 'lesser of $50,000 (less any higher loan balance you carried in the past 12 months) or the greater of half your vested balance or $10,000, minus loans already outstanding'. Read literally the trailing subtraction applies to the whole lesser-of, double-deducting outstanding loans from the $50,000 prong (example: vested 200,000, outstanding 10,000, highest 10,000: statute gives 40,000, the sentence gives 30,000). The engine fixtures in the brief are right (highest 50,000, outstanding 20,000 gives A=20,000 and max new loan 0), but the answer string is copied verbatim into the writer prompt and the section 1 answer block, so it must be fixed before approval. (3) Evidence gaps for the solo claim: the extract lacks 4975(c)(1)(B) (lending of money between a plan and a disqualified person is the prohibited transaction that makes the IRA-plan 'cannot lend' statement true), and the answer lists 4975(d)(1) conditions as only (plan provision, reasonable rate, adequately secured) while the statute also requires (A) reasonably equivalent availability and (B) no larger amounts for highly compensated employees. (4) Duplicate/cannibalization: coverage.txt re-read; only /guides/401k-loan-rules (rules explainer, existing formula and three worked examples, no computing tool), /compare/401k-loan-vs-heloc (borrowing-path choice), /compare/sep-ira-vs-solo-401k (plan choice, one sentence that solo plans can lend), /loan-payment-calculator (generic payment only, no statutory cap) and /compare/bridge-loan-vs-heloc (product choice) are nearby. I also grepped src/data for 'hard money' and found no occurrence; 'bridge loan' appears only in the comparison. All have a different reader goal from a calculator; no same-intent page exists. TL-01 is not narrowed to enrichment-only: 401k loan calculator 4,400/mo KD29 (volumes3.json, SEMRUSH us, verified row by row against the saved JSON) is a real calculator-intent gap and the guide cannot compute a cap or payment. TL-02 vs TL-03: different SERP heads (hard money loan calculator 1,900 vs bridge loan calculator 1,600), different readers (investor financing a flip vs homeowner buying before selling) and different outputs (LTC, LTARV, flip profit vs overlap outlay, net proceeds); merging would lose a 1,600/mo head, so both stay, with the Phase 1 advisory cannibalization check retained. findings.problem: The TL-01 answer sentence (action.answer, newPageBriefs[0].readerAndAnswer.answer, presented as the section 1 answer block) says the cap is 'the lesser of $50,000 (less any higher loan balance you carried in the past 12 months) or the greater of half your vested balance or $10,000, minus loans already outstanding'. The trailing 'minus loans already outstanding' attaches to the whole lesser-of and double-deducts outstanding loans from the $50,000 prong. Under 26 USC 72(p)(2)(A) the new loan plus all outstanding loans must not exceed min(50,000 - (highest12 - outstanding), max(vested/2, 10,000)), i.e. max new loan = min(50,000 - highest12, max(vested/2, 10,000) - outstanding).
findings.fix: Rewrite the answer in both places (they must stay identical) with the exact two-prong form, for example: 'Your new loan, added to loans you already owe the plan, cannot exceed the lesser of $50,000 reduced by how much your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded your balance today, or the greater of half your vested balance or $10,000; the calculator subtracts what you already owe and returns the largest new loan and the payment for the amount you enter.' Add an engine fixture with outstanding > 0 and highest12 > outstanding where the double-deduction would differ (for example vested 200,000, outstanding 10,000, highest12 20,000: statute gives min(50,000 - 20,000, 100,000 - 10,000) = 30,000; the faulty reading gives 20,000) to the brief's engine and boundaries text. Check the outline's worked-case section and the TL-04 guide section use the same wording. Re-hash the manifest and readiness afterward.

findings.problem: The TL-01 and TL-04 answers present the 26 USC 4975(d)(1) conditions as '(provided for in the plan, reasonable interest rate, adequately secured)'. The statute lists five conditions: (A) available to all participants on a reasonably equivalent basis, (B) not made available to highly compensated employees in a greater amount than to other employees, (C) made under specific plan provisions, (D) reasonable rate of interest, (E) adequately secured. Presenting three as the full set understates the boundary of a yes-with-conditions verdict on a YMYL page.
findings.fix: Word the answer as 'conditions that include...' or list all five in the closed fact list and say the plan document and its administrator decide whether a given loan meets them. Keep the no-provider-claims limit. Update both action rows and the TL-01 brief, and apply the same wording in the TL-04 section/FAQ plan.

findings.problem: The statement that an IRA-based plan (SEP, SIMPLE, traditional IRA) cannot lend to its owner rests on 26 USC 4975(c)(1)(B) (lending of money or other extension of credit between a plan and a disqualified person is a prohibited transaction) together with 4975(f)(6)(A)(i) and (B)(i)(II)-(III) and (B)(iii). research/statute-extracts.md contains (d)(1) and (f)(6) but not (c)(1)(B), so the central consequential conclusion is not fully grounded in the saved evidence. Per _workflow-checkpoints (rpa-prepare-answer-and-scope) a source the proposed answer depends on is preparation, not a Phase 3 fetch.
findings.fix: Add the 4975(c)(1)(B) text (live on Cornell LII, HTTP 200 on 2026-11-14; I verified it reads 'lending of money or other extension of credit between a plan and a disqualified person') and the 4975(f)(6)(B)(i)(II)-(III)/(iii) interplay to research/statute-extracts.md, rehash it in manifest evidenceFiles and every brief's evidenceFiles, and cite (c)(1)(B) in the closed facts for the IRA-plan sentence. Keep the source-silence rule: say the statute text bars the exemption for IRA owners and that plan documents control for solo 401(k)s; do not assert anything about specific providers.

findings.problem: Strongest plausible counterexample to a reader-friendly 'solo owners can borrow' takeaway: 72(p)(3)(B)(i) denies the interest deduction from the first day the borrower is a key employee, and 26 USC 416(i)(1)(A)(ii) makes a 5-percent owner a key employee (text verified live). A solo 401(k) owner will normally be one, so the interest-deductibility condition is decision-relevant and the existing guide already states the key-employee restriction.
findings.fix: Either add the 416(i)(1)(A)(ii) text to the closed fact list and one sentence that an owner is generally a key employee so interest on the owner's own loan is not deductible, or link the guide's interest-deductibility section and make no deductibility claim. Do not imply deductibility.
